title: Prescribing values of independent split-torus characters
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $T$ be an affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ for every commutative $F$-algebra $A$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $m\geq0$ and let $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_m:T\to\mathbf G_m$ be group-scheme homomorphisms. Assume these characters are $\mathbf Z$-linearly independent: an identity $\prod_{i=1}^m\chi_i^{n_i}=1$ of characters, for integers $n_i$, implies $n_i=0$ for every $i$. For every $(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(F^\times)^m$, there exists $t\in T(F)$ such that $\chi_i(t)=c_i$ for every $i$. The assertion includes $m=0$ and $r=0$, and places no restriction on the characteristic.

source.place: Proposition 23.7, printed p.486, choice of the torus element with specified simple-root values; Theorem 12.9(a), printed pp.233--234. The independent-character generalization over an algebraically closed field is the lattice extension argument underlying this choice; written by the agent, rather than asserted as the literal statement of 12.9.

proof.text: Choose $\iota:\mathbf G_m^r\xrightarrow{\sim}T$. By [lem-sfb-split-torus-hom-matrices], each $\chi_i\circ\iota$ has an exponent vector $u_i\in L=\mathbf Z^r$, with value $\prod_k x_k^{u_{ik}}$. The correspondence is an isomorphism of abelian groups, so independence of the characters implies independence of the $u_i$. Put $N=\sum_i\mathbf Zu_i\subseteq L$. Each element of $N$ has a unique expression $\sum_i n_i u_i$: subtract two expressions and use independence. Thus $h_N(\sum_i n_i u_i)=\prod_i c_i^{n_i}$ is a well-defined homomorphism $N\to F^\times$, with $h_N(u_i)=c_i$.

source.place: Proposition 23.7, printed p.486, prescribed simple-root values; Theorem 12.9(a), printed pp.233--234. Agent-written lattice-extension argument for independent characters.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-pid-submodule-smith-bases] with $R=\mathbf Z$, ambient module $L$ with its standard finite basis, and submodules $N\subseteq O=L$. Obtain $n\leq o$, a basis $b_1,\ldots,b_o$ of $L$ and a basis $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $N$, with $v_j=a_jb_j$ for integers $a_j$. Every $a_j$ is nonzero: otherwise $v_j=0$, contrary to linear independence of a basis. No identification of $n$ with $m$ or of $o$ with $r$ is needed.

source.place: Agent lattice-extension argument underlying Milne Proposition 23.7, p.486; Smith bases are the cited Mathlib leaf Submodule.exists_smith_normal_form_of_le, Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/FreeModule/PID.lean:492--497.

proof.text: For $1\leq j\leq n$ set $d_j=h_N(v_j)\in F^\times$. If $a_j>0$, choose a root $w_j$ of $X^{a_j}-d_j$; if $a_j<0$, choose a root of $X^{-a_j}-d_j^{-1}$. Such a root exists by [def-weil-algebraic-closure], since the exponent is positive and the polynomial is nonconstant. Its nonzero constant term ensures $w_j\ne0$. In either case $w_j^{a_j}=d_j$. For $n<j\leq o$ set $w_j=1$. This uses existence of roots only, also when the characteristic divides $a_j$.

source.place: Proposition 23.7, printed p.486, prescribed simple-root values; Theorem 12.9(a), printed pp.233--234. Agent-written lattice-extension argument for independent characters.

proof.text: Define $h:L\to F^\times$ on the unique basis expansion by $h(\sum_{j=1}^o k_jb_j)=\prod_{j=1}^o w_j^{k_j}$. Adding expansions and the integer-power law show that $h$ is a homomorphism. For $j\leq n$, $h(v_j)=w_j^{a_j}=d_j=h_N(v_j)$. For any $v=\sum_{j=1}^n l_jv_j\in N$, therefore $h(v)=\prod_j h(v_j)^{l_j}=\prod_j h_N(v_j)^{l_j}=h_N(v)$. Thus $h$ extends $h_N$.

source.place: Proposition 23.7, printed p.486, prescribed simple-root values; Theorem 12.9(a), printed pp.233--234. Agent-written lattice-extension argument for independent characters.

proof.text: Let $e_1,\ldots,e_r$ be the standard basis of $L$, set $x_k=h(e_k)\in F^\times$ and $t=\iota_F((x_k)_k)$. The monomial formula of [lem-sfb-split-torus-hom-matrices] gives $\chi_i(t)=\prod_k h(e_k)^{u_{ik}}=h(u_i)=h_N(u_i)=c_i$. If $m=0$, all conditions are empty and the construction still works (the identity point suffices). If $r=0$, every exponent vector is zero, so independence forces $m=0$ and the unique point suffices.
